name: Misattribution of memory
statement: People recall content accurately and assign it to the wrong origin, so a face, a fact or an idea from one occasion is remembered as belonging to another.
meaning: Source is not stored as a label fixed to a memory and read off when the memory returns. The central claim of Johnson, Hashtroudi and Lindsay's review is that activated memory records are evaluated and attributed to particular sources through decision processes performed during remembering. Those decisions run on qualities of what comes back: perceptual information such as sound and colour, spatial and temporal context, semantic detail, affective information, and records of the cognitive operations that formed the memory. Memories of perceived events carry, on average, more perceptual and contextual detail and fewer traces of mental effort than memories of imagined ones, and the judgement exploits that average difference. Most attributions are fast and undeliberate. Some are slow, and draw on plausibility and on what the person otherwise knows. Because the decision compares distributions rather than reading a tag, two sources that resemble each other are confusable. The framework splits the problem three ways. Reality monitoring separates what was perceived from what was imagined. External source monitoring separates one outside source from another, such as which of two speakers said a thing. Internal source monitoring separates what was thought from what was said aloud. Schacter and Dodson group the resulting failures under misattribution, one of seven memory sins alongside transience, absent-mindedness, blocking, suggestibility, bias and persistence.

origin.who: Marcia K. Johnson, Shahin Hashtroudi and D. Stephen Lindsay
origin.note: The paper is a review, not an experiment. It states that the source-monitoring framework extends the reality-monitoring framework Johnson and Raye proposed in 1981, which separated memories of perceived events from memories of imagined ones, to source discriminations of every kind. Its abstract lists the phenomena it means to cover: old-new recognition, indirect tests, eyewitness testimony, misattributed familiarity, cryptomnesia, and incorporation of fiction into fact. Schacter's misattribution label, which groups these errors with false recognition, came later.

evidence: The 1993 review sets out paradigms rather than reporting new data. The case it treats at length is Jacoby's fame-judgement task, described here from Johnson, Hashtroudi and Lindsay's account rather than from the original papers. Participants read a list of nonfamous names, then judged fame for a list mixing those names, new nonfamous names and famous ones, after being told that every name on the first list was nonfamous. Tested at once, they called the old nonfamous names famous less often than the new ones. Tested after a delay, they called them famous more often. Familiarity had outlasted the memory of where it came from. Jacoby, Woloshyn and Kelley then had some participants listen for runs of three odd numbers while reading the first list. Divided attention lowered old-new recognition and left the fame error unchanged, even when participants were told to call any remembered name nonfamous. Dywan and Jacoby ran the task with two age groups, and older participants made the fame error more often than younger ones. The pooled numbers come from eyewitness research. Deffenbacher, Bornstein and Penrod collected 11 published articles from 1977 to 2003 giving 32 independent tests of whether mugshot exposure damages a later lineup identification, with 1664 participants and samples from 26 to 276. They then collected seven articles giving 19 independent tests of the transference hypothesis, with 1145 participants and samples from 24 to 165. A transference design puts a face into the lineup that the witness saw near the target in time, either in mugshots or as a bystander at the event. Across the 19 tests, transference errors ran at .33 against .16 in control conditions. The unweighted metaanalytic Z was 9.24, p < .0001, with a failsafe N of 581 studies; weighting by sample size gave Z = 8.89 and a failsafe N of 537. Mean effect size for the unweighted analysis was h = +.34, 95% CI +.08 to +.60, median +.35. The tests were heterogeneous, chi-squared(18) = 64.58, p < .001. Splitting them, the 11 designs using mugshots gave error rates of .38 against .16 and h = +.44, 95% CI +.11 to +.77. The eight bystander designs gave .27 against .17 and h = +.19, 95% CI −.33 to +.71. Simple retroactive interference, where neither the target nor any mugshot face appeared in the lineup, did not reliably reduce accuracy: h = −.12, 95% CI −.55 to +.31. What did damage accuracy was committing to a face. Where witnesses had identified someone from the mugshots, proportion correct fell to .32 from .55, h = −.48, and the lineup false alarm rate rose to .53 from .20, h = +.72, 95% CI +.38 to +1.06. Beyond the courtroom, Damiani and six colleagues screened 5,256 records and meta-analysed 44 studies comparing source monitoring in psychosis against healthy controls, 1566 patients and 1175 controls. Performance was worse across all measures, SMD = 0.458, CI 0.401 to 0.514. Errors were larger for internally generated sources, SMD = 0.513, CI 0.315 to 0.711, than for external ones, SMD = 0.398, CI 0.226 to 0.570. The largest gap was for imagined stimuli, where accuracy gave SMD = 0.978, CI 0.688 to 1.268.

replication.headline: Pooling 19 independent tests and 1145 participants, a face seen near the target in time is misidentified at a lineup about twice as often as a face that was not, and the pooled interval excludes zero.
replication.detail: Deffenbacher, Bornstein and Penrod's third metaanalysis is the sturdiest number in this literature. Transference errors ran at .33 against a control rate of .16, mean h = +.34 with a 95% interval of +.08 to +.60, and a failsafe N of 581 studies averaging null results. Cohen's h is not one of the metrics this site's structured fields accept, so the figure is quoted here and left out of them. The pooled result hides a split. Transference produced by mugshot exposure gave h = +.44 with an interval clear of zero, while the bystander version gave h = +.19 with an interval running from −.33 to +.71. Lindsay, writing in 2014, calls the bystander evidence the more mixed of the two and points at a rival explanation. Davis, Loftus, Vanous and Cucciare filmed an innocent person walking down a grocery aisle, hid him behind a stack of boxes, and had a different person emerge and steal a bottle. Many viewers did not notice the swap, and those who did not were the ones who went on to identify the innocent man. Lindsay's reading is that change blindness accounts for some apparent bystander misidentification and that source confusion accounts for some of the rest. A second, independent meta-analysis reaches the same construct from clinical work: Damiani and colleagues put the psychosis-control gap in source monitoring at SMD = 0.458, CI 0.401 to 0.514, over 44 studies. No preregistered multi-site replication of any source-monitoring paradigm was located.

study.cite: Deffenbacher, K. A., Bornstein, B. H., & Penrod, S. D. (2006). Mugshot exposure effects: Retroactive interference, mugshot commitment, source confusion, and unconscious transference. Law and Human Behavior, 30(3), 287-307.

limits: The claim is about attribution, and it is measured almost entirely on faces and word lists. Deffenbacher and colleagues bound their own result carefully. Their sample stops at 2003, their transference tests are heterogeneous, and the metric is Cohen's h on proportions rather than a standardised mean difference. Their age comparison is the weakest thing in the paper and is often quoted as the strongest. Older witnesses made transference errors at .57 against .30 for younger ones, but the older figure rests on three effect sizes from one article, Perfect and Harris, and h = +.85 carries a 95% interval from −.52 to +2.22. The authors say the result should be interpreted with caution, and this page repeats that rather than the point estimate. The two meta-analyses that carry the age evidence properly could not be read. Spencer and Raz pooled 46 studies and report that age differences in context memory are reliably greater than those in memory for content. Old and Naveh-Benjamin pooled 90 studies with 3,197 young and 3,192 older adults. They report an age-related associative deficit covering source, context, temporal order, spatial location and item pairings. Both are paywalled, both abstracts are silent on effect sizes, and no citing paper reached here quoted one. Fraundorf and colleagues excluded source memory tasks from their own ageing meta-analysis and named those two as the ones that cover the ground. The search ran across Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, PubMed, Europe PMC and the open web. Johnson, Hashtroudi and Lindsay was read from a page-image scan hosted by Yale, which carries no text layer and was transcribed here by optical character recognition, so only its wording is used and none of its numbers. Jacoby, Kelley, Brown and Jasechko's original fame paper, Jacoby, Woloshyn and Kelley, Dywan and Jacoby, Davis and colleagues, and Perfect and Harris were all paywalled and are described at one remove from the reviews that discuss them. Schacter's 1999 article was likewise paywalled; the list of seven sins is taken from Schacter and Dodson's abstract. Damiani and colleagues studied psychosis, and their effect sizes say nothing about the size of the error in a healthy population.
misreadings: The first misreading is that this is cryptomnesia. It is not, and the two entries divide cleanly. Cryptomnesia requires the mark of pastness to be gone, so a borrowed idea arrives feeling invented. Misattribution leaves the item marked as remembered and moves only its origin. The second is that this is false memory. Implantation studies build an event that never happened; misattribution takes a real one and files it in the wrong place. The third is the mugshot. Showing a witness photographs is widely said to spoil a later identification, and the pooled evidence does not say that. Where the target was absent from both the mugshots and the lineup, the effect on accuracy was h = −.12 with an interval from −.55 to +.31. The damage came from commitment: witnesses who picked someone out of the mugshots then picked at .53 from a lineup where the correct answer was absent, against .20 for controls. The fourth is that unconscious transference is settled. The bystander form of it, which is the form the courtroom argument is usually about, has a pooled interval that includes zero. Davis and colleagues showed that viewers who failed to notice one person replacing another produce the same pattern of errors. The fifth is treating the divided-attention result as showing that inattention causes the error. What Jacoby, Woloshyn and Kelley found, on Johnson, Hashtroudi and Lindsay's account, is that dividing attention at encoding left the fame error where it was while lowering ordinary recognition. Source attribution and item recognition come apart, which is the whole point of the framework and the reason a witness can be certain of a face and wrong about where it was seen.

sources.text: Johnson, M. K., Hashtroudi, S., & Lindsay, D. S. (1993). Source monitoring. Psychological Bulletin, 114(1), 3-28. The framework paper. Read in full from the page-image scan hosted by Yale's memory lab, transcribed by optical character recognition; the source for the framework's claims, the fame-judgement description and the ageing summary, and for no number on this page.

Deffenbacher, K. A., Bornstein, B. H., & Penrod, S. D. (2006). Mugshot exposure effects: Retroactive interference, mugshot commitment, source confusion, and unconscious transference. Law and Human Behavior, 30(3), 287-307. Read in full from the author copy at DigitalCommons@UNO; the source for every meta-analytic figure in the eyewitness paragraphs.

Damiani, S., Donadeo, A., Bassetti, N., Salazar-de-Pablo, G., Guiot, C., Politi, P., & Fusar-Poli, P. (2022). Understanding source monitoring subtypes and their relation to psychosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Psychiatry and Clinical Neurosciences, 76(5), 162-171. Open access and read in full; the source for the psychosis effect sizes.

Lindsay, D. S. (2014). Memory source monitoring applied. In T. J. Perfect & D. S. Lindsay (eds), The SAGE Handbook of Applied Memory, pp. 59-75. London: SAGE. Read in full from the copy on the author's University of Victoria site; the source for the change-blindness critique and for the judgement that the bystander evidence is mixed.

Schacter, D. L., & Dodson, C. S. (2001). Misattribution, false recognition and the sins of memory. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London B, 356(1413), 1385-1393. Abstract read at PubMed Central; the source for the list of seven sins and for misattribution's place in it. The full text was not obtained.

Schacter, D. L. (1999). The seven sins of memory: Insights from psychology and cognitive neuroscience. American Psychologist, 54(3), 182-203. The article that named the seven sins. Metadata verified at Crossref; the article itself is paywalled and was not read.

Jacoby, L. L., Kelley, C., Brown, J., & Jasechko, J. (1989). Becoming famous overnight: Limits on the ability to avoid unconscious influences of the past. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 56(3), 326-338. The fame-judgement paradigm. Metadata verified at Crossref; paywalled, and described here from Johnson, Hashtroudi and Lindsay's account of it.

Davis, D., Loftus, E. F., Vanous, S., & Cucciare, M. (2008). 'Unconscious transference' can be an instance of 'change blindness'. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 22(5), 605-623. Metadata verified at Crossref; paywalled, and described here from Lindsay's account of it.

Perfect, T. J., & Harris, L. J. (2003). Adult age differences in unconscious transference: Source confusion or identity blending? Memory & Cognition, 31(4), 570-580. The single article supplying the three older-adult effect sizes in Deffenbacher's age analysis. Metadata verified at Crossref; not read here.

Spencer, W. D., & Raz, N. (1995). Differential effects of aging on memory for content and context: A meta-analysis. Psychology and Aging, 10(4), 527-539. Abstract read at PubMed. It reports 46 studies and states that age differences in context memory are reliably greater than in memory for content. No effect size appears in the abstract and the full text is paywalled.

Old, S. R., & Naveh-Benjamin, M. (2008). Differential effects of age on item and associative measures of memory: A meta-analysis. Psychology and Aging, 23(1), 104-118. Abstract read at PubMed. It reports 90 studies with 3,197 young and 3,192 older adults and an associative deficit covering source, context, temporal order, spatial location and item pairings. No effect size appears in the abstract and the full text is paywalled.

Fraundorf, S. H., Hourihan, K. L., Peters, R. A., & Benjamin, A. S. (2019). Aging and recognition memory: A meta-analysis. Psychological Bulletin, 145(4), 339-371. Read in full from the author copy at the University of Illinois. Cited only for its statement that it excluded source memory tasks and that Old and Naveh-Benjamin (2008) and Spencer and Raz (1995) cover them.
